title: The little explain-it garden
intro: No secret engineer handshake needed. A dotted-underlined technical word is a tiny door: click it to land on its explanation. Every repeated matching word or phrase works, including captions. Use your PDF viewer's Back command to return; in the offline reader, use browser Back. The alphabetical map and subject gardens offer another way in. These little analogies explain the journal, not extra features or promises.

groups.title: Faces, shapes and tiny building blocks

terms.explanation: Imagine a face made from a fishing net. Tiny connected points and patches describe its shape. Verona draws and moves this digital net; 'face mesh' here does not mean a camera is watching your face.
A vertex is one little dot in the net. Vertices is the plural. Moving the dots changes the face, rather like nudging the pins in a soft toy's pattern.

A mesh edge joins two dots; a contour follows an outline, like pencil lines on a paper face. 'Edge' also names Microsoft's web browser in the testing notes. That browser is not a piece of facial geometry.

Dots join into small flat patches: three corners make a triangle, four make a quad. Lots of tiny paper patches can look curved together. A drawn rectangular grid does not magically turn the underlying triangles into quads.

Topology says which dots are connected, not just where they sit. Two dots can be close without being sewn together, like the two sides of closed lips. Retopology means making a different connection pattern.

Native means 'belongs to the original thing' in this sentence. Native head geometry keeps that head's own dots; a native desktop window belongs to Windows. It does not mean more realistic or automatically more accurate.
Each dot keeps its own name tag: this dot is always the same bit of lip. Matching name tags let old motion dress a reshaped face. Equal dot counts alone do not prove the name tags match.

This is the face's relaxed starting shape, like a puppet resting on the table. 'Rest-space' measurements use that starting map. Neutral is a model setting, not proof that a person would read the face as emotionless.
A pose is one complete arrangement of the face's dots. A little flipbook of poses becomes motion. A still pose cannot tell us whether the whole movement looks natural.

Deformation gently changes a shape, like squeezing soft clay. A structural map tells each point how to move. Verona can apply the same map to whole poses; that is not the same as training a new face model.

A rig is a puppet's control system. Joints are turnable handles; blendshapes are prepared alternate shapes you can mix. A static imported head does not arrive with useful mouth controls just because it looks like a face.

Retargeting teaches one puppet to follow another puppet's moves. An adapter translates between their different shapes. A broad smile may transfer well while delicate lip contact gets lost: the puppets do not share every handle.

A hybrid mixes two ingredients. The Claire-based experiments keep Claire's named dots while borrowing some shape from another head, like using one cookie cutter with a different icing design. This does not create another trained network.

Geometry is the actual digital shape; skin is the face surface we move. Paint and lighting sit on top, like coloring a balloon. Verona also calls its filled-patch presentation Surface; that is a drawing choice, not another shape.

A silhouette is the outside outline, like a shadow cutout. Proportions are how big the parts are compared with each other. A larger eye or narrower chin can change a character even before any paint is added.
Anatomy is how real body parts are built and meet. A model's lips touching in one picture is not proof they behave like real lips throughout speech. Our digital puppet still needs careful checking.

The aperture is the little opening between the eyelids. The orbital area is the neighborhood around the eye. Akari's lashes must sit along that actual opening, like trim sewn onto the edge of a tiny curtain.
The sclera is the white part of an eye; the iris is its colored ring, around the dark pupil. Verona draws eye surfaces and effects, not a fully simulated biological eye with every moving part.
Cupid's bow is the little double curve at the middle of the upper lip. A rim is a boundary edge. The nape is the back of the neck. These are useful landmarks for fitting our tiny digital face.

Identity is which face a recipe and its matching assets describe. Calibration measures where useful features belong, like finding eyes before fitting glasses. Landmarks are those useful reference locations, not proof that the face has a complete biological rig.

terms.term: Lip guide / lip seal / wide opening
terms.explanation: A lip guide traces the mouth. Outer lips and folded inner edges can move differently. A seal fills a tiny closed-mouth gap; a wide-opening rule waits for enough opening before clearing pixels. The goal is touching lips at rest, not an always-open slit.
Coordinates are an address for a point. X goes sideways, Y up or down, and Z in or out in the chosen system. An axis is one measuring direction: a tiny three-way ruler.
Rotation turns something. For a head, yaw is 'no', pitch is 'yes', and roll tilts an ear toward a shoulder. In audio, 'pitch' instead means how high or low a sound is; context matters.
These are two rulers for turns. A full turn is 360 degrees or two times pi radians. Mixing the rulers is like using teaspoons when the recipe says cups: the result can be wildly wrong.
A scalar is one number, such as a mouth-opening amount. A vector is an ordered bundle of numbers. A coefficient is a mixing amount, like how many spoonfuls of one shape ingredient to use.

A delta is a change from a starting value; displacement is a point's move. Gain makes a change stronger or weaker. Halving Rowan's expression gain halves that extra expression movement, not the whole face or audio.

Interpolation fills the gap between known poses, like drawing the flipbook page between two pages. Smoothing softens sudden changes. Neither trick invents better speech understanding or guarantees perfectly natural movement.
The mean adds values and shares them equally; the median is the middle one after sorting. With 1, 2 and 99, the median is 2. That helps a few odd lip points avoid bossing the measurement around.

Principal component analysis, or PCA, packs many shapes into a small recipe: a starting shape plus reusable change directions called a basis. Reconstruction mixes the recipe back into dots. Recipes from different heads are not interchangeable.
A parabola is a smooth U-like curve. An ellipse is a stretched circle; oval is a looser everyday shape word. Verona uses gentle curves as guides, but a neat curve alone cannot know a real lip or jaw.

Imagine shining a very thin flashlight beam into the model. A ray test finds which surface that beam meets. Comparing eye and skin hits helps find the real visible eyelid edge instead of guessing an arc nearby.

Find a boundary by repeatedly cutting a bracket in half, like a 'warmer or colder' game with two known ends. Eighteen cuts locate the eye edge much more closely; they do not prove every eye pose is perfect.

Picture a tiny hammock tied to three triangle corners. Three nonnegative shares that add to one say where you sit inside it. Those shares let an attached lash follow the triangle without wandering beyond its supporting corners.

An axis-aligned bounding box, or AABB, is a simple box around geometry. Boxes help skip faraway triangles, like looking in the right toy drawer first. The final nearest-triangle calculation is still exact in this study.

Fitting lines up two shapes so matching features meet, like adjusting a paper mask to a face. A similarity alignment can move, turn and uniformly resize it. Good alignment does not create missing facial controls.

Welding joins matching boundary dots for a calculation, like temporarily pinning a dress seam. A neck skirt extends a boundary downward to help fitting. Here these helpers are not secretly added to the delivered head's topology.

A Jacobian describes how a tiny patch stretches, turns or flips when its shape changes. A mathematical derivative measures such change. It is a local cloth-folding check, not proof the whole face has no collisions or overlapping parts.

Falloff makes an effect fade gently with distance. Taper makes a strand thinner toward its tip. Clearance leaves breathing room between objects. Too much clearance can make hair float like a loose helmet.

Projection turns a 3D shape into a flat picture, like a shadow on a wall. Perspective makes nearer parts look larger. Symmetric lipstick on the model need not occupy equal-looking areas when the head turns.

Quantization rounds many possible values into fewer little buckets. Think of measuring with a ruler marked only in millimeters. Small differences can appear even when the underlying motion is very close; the bucket size matters.

A threshold is the line a value must cross to do something. A bound is a limit; clamping keeps values inside it. A mouth-opening gate is like a tiny door rule, not evidence that every mouth looks right.

Mirrored guides use matching left and right measurements, like folding a paper heart. They help keep lipstick placement balanced. Real expressions, the underlying head and a turned camera can still look different on the two sides.

groups.title: How the picture reaches your screen

terms.explanation: The renderer is the little scene painter: it turns geometry and colors into screen pixels. Rasterization decides which pixels each shape covers. Tiny outline pixels may vary even when the intended face and settings are unchanged.
Pixels are the tiny colored squares in an image. Resolution tells how many squares it has. Higher density can make an image sharper, but costs work; more squares do not repair a wrong shape.
A frame is one picture in a moving flipbook. FPS means frames per second. New face poses can arrive at 30 per second while a display draws 60, filling between them; those are different jobs.
The viewport is the little window through which the scene is drawn. Framing decides what fits; zoom makes the head look bigger. A bigger face may need a bigger window so its hair is not cut off.

A crop chooses the visible area. Clipping rejects things outside a boundary; a mask controls where drawing is allowed. Think of a paper stencil. Hiding shoulders on screen is not always the same as reducing geometry work.
A shader is a small program the graphics chip runs while drawing. A uniform is a shared setting it reads, like a color knob. One knob can change the look without rebuilding the whole puppet.
The graphics processing unit, or GPU, is a helper that draws many tiny pieces together. WebGL2 lets the browser ask it to draw. It is not necessarily the same helper running the speech network.

The central processing unit, or CPU, is the computer's general-purpose worker. A core is one working unit inside it. AMD is one maker. A percentage of one core is not automatically the percentage of the entire computer.

A buffer is a labeled tray of numbers or sound samples. An index buffer lists which dots form triangles. Upload sends a tray to another owner; readback brings it back. A GPU upload is not necessarily an internet upload.

A normal is a tiny arrow telling which way a surface faces; lighting uses it to shade the face. Material describes how it should look. Here 'normal opacity' means the ordinary opacity setting, not a surface arrow.

Toon shading uses cartoon-like light bands. A clay view removes decorative color so the shape is easier to inspect. Cosmetics are surface styling such as lipstick; they do not guarantee that the lips underneath meet correctly.
RGB stores red, green and blue; alpha adds how much shows through. Opaque means not see-through. A transparent mouth clears the background in its cutout; it does not add a realistic mouth interior.

Depth tells which thing is closer to the viewer. A depth test helps the front thing hide the back thing, called occlusion. Like a hand hiding a cookie, a front triangle can stop another layer being painted.

Compositing combines drawing layers, like stacking clear picture sheets. A pass is one drawing step. Clearing only one mouth layer can reveal the back of the head, so the order and depth rules matter.

A filled Surface view paints patches; wireframe shows their connecting lines. Verona's FaceMesh presentation is a front triangular look with special eye styling. Choosing another drawing style does not load a second speech brain.

FaceDot sprinkles visible round marks over the surface. UniformPolygons draws a regular-looking grid in surface coordinates. They are outfits for the same moving face, not new neural models or a secretly rebuilt quad rig.

Procedural means made by a recipe rather than hand-placing every piece. Hair locks are little shaped strands; a quiff sweeps short hair upward. Verona's selected hair shares the existing renderer and does not grow new geometry every frame.

A few useful points describe the space a head and hair need, like measuring a hat before putting it in a box. A combined fit leaves room for both. It must include the real hair tips, not a guessed sphere.

A palette is a small box of allowed colors. Encoding packs pictures into a file; decoding opens the package. Delta encoding saves changes between pictures, like writing only what changed on the next flipbook page.
Branding is the app's visual name tag. A wordmark styles the name; a lockup arranges name and symbol together. Audiowide is a typeface used in Verona's mark, not a speech model or an audio feature.
2D is flat; 3D has depth. A canvas is a drawing area, and a desktop overlay is a window shown over other windows. A transparent overlay does not automatically capture the apps behind it.

Per-vertex paint stores color at mesh dots. Continuous cosmetic rules describe color smoothly between locations, like a steady crayon stroke instead of a handful of stickers. Good paint still cannot fix an incorrectly shaped mouth.
Animation changes a picture over time. A trajectory is a planned path; a field says how a region of points should move. Picture a tiny dance map, not an invisible person deciding how to feel.

The audio clock tells where playback really is. The face follows that clock, like a dancer following the music rather than a separate stopwatch. Pause, seek and replay must keep both partners together.

RequestAnimationFrame, or RAF, asks the browser for the next drawing turn. A loop asks again after each turn. Stopping that loop while a head sleeps avoids painting the same quiet puppet over and over.

A timer is an alarm. A timeout rings once; an interval repeats. A scheduler decides when jobs may run. Verona's local idle scheduler picks occasional gestures without asking the chat to choose each one.

Weighted selection gives some choices more raffle tickets. A cooldown makes a choice wait before trying again. A 10% sound chance is not exactly one in every ten. Elsewhere, model weights mean its learned numbers, not raffle tickets.

Idle means not actively speaking or being controlled. Idle life adds occasional local gestures. A performance-only head instead rests quietly until speech wakes it; the warm speech model can still occupy memory while the drawing naps.

An event is a little 'something happened' note, such as playback ending. A controller updates the current state from those notes. Event-driven code waits for a useful note rather than constantly asking 'are we there yet?'.

Cancellation asks a job to stop or discards its result. Preemption lets a more important job take over, like speech interrupting an idle yawn. Already-running neural work may finish before its unwanted result can be thrown away.

Inspection lets you stop and examine a pose. Replay starts a clip again; seeking jumps within it. A paused mouth should not be borrowed by an idle gesture while you are carefully studying the frozen picture.

The cursor is your mouse pointer; gaze is the direction the eyes appear to look. Verona can move eyes or the whole head toward it. This is a visual effect, not proof of eye-joint physics or knowledge of what you are viewing.

A blink briefly closes the lids. Optical closure also makes the drawn eye stop showing through. Closing skin while leaving a glowing eye floating on top would be like shutting a curtain but painting the window over it.
A phase is one part of a movement: starting, strongest point, or settling. A pulse rises and falls. A neutral hold pauses at the relaxed face so viewers can see where a gesture begins and ends.

Finite means there is an end or a limit. Per-frame work repeats for each picture; generation creates output. Making a hairstyle once and drawing it many times is much cheaper than baking a fresh hairstyle for every flipbook page.

groups.title: Voices and the little sound kitchen

terms.explanation: Text-to-speech, or TTS, turns written words into sound. System.Speech is the local Windows voice system used here. Synthesized means made by a system; it does not mean recorded from a real person in this session.

A trained model is a learned recipe stored as numbers. Verona has different jobs: one recipe can make voice, another can predict face motion from audio. A head name or a drawing outfit is not automatically another learned recipe.

Training makes a learned recipe; inference uses it. Conditioning gives it extra instructions, like an identity or expression setting. Combining two instructions is not necessarily the same as averaging two separately baked results.

An expression channel is a named control such as Angry. Explicit means the app sets it deliberately. A label is not mind-reading: the puppet moving when Angry is set does not prove people recognize anger or that the system feels it.

A phoneme is a speech sound unit; a viseme is a visible mouth-shape grouping. Articulation is how speech movements form sounds. A talking face can move smoothly yet still make the wrong lip shape for a word.

A phonemizer translates text into speech-sound symbols, like writing a pronunciation recipe. eSpeak supplies tools used in that job. Its software license is separate from the license for a voice model's learned numbers.

Kokoro is Verona's optional local speech engine. Its installed pack offers many voice styles using one lazily loaded model per requesting head. INT8 stores many numbers in small 8-bit buckets to reduce their size.

Pulse-code modulation, or PCM, stores a sound wave as a row of measurements called samples. Mono has one channel; stereo has two. In an image test, 'sample' instead means one chosen observation, not necessarily a sound measurement.

Sample rate says how many sound measurements arrive each second. Hz means per second; kHz means thousands per second. A stride is the step between analyzed windows, like moving a little magnifying glass along the sound ribbon.
Trimming removes an unwanted beginning or ending. A fade gently turns the sound up or down, like easing a tiny volume knob rather than snapping it. Duration is how long the remaining clip lasts.

Volume changes loudness; mute makes playback silent. A gain cap limits the allowed multiplier, not guaranteed measured loudness. Equalization, or EQ, adjusts low and high sound regions, like seasoning different parts of a sound soup.

Speech Synthesis Markup Language, or SSML, wraps text with speaking instructions. Pitch changes high versus low sound; emphasis stresses a part. Unsupported controls must be disabled or rejected, not pretended to work.

An effect is a prepared little sound such as a sneeze. Voice matching chooses an existing clip from metadata; it does not clone the speaker. Permission to play a supplied recording locally is not permission to publish it.

This means someone actually listens and judges the intended sound quality or timing. Silent browser tests can check playback events and numbers, but cannot tell us that a voice sounded good. Ears are still invited to that party.

Audio is sound information; a voice is a chosen speaking sound. A clip is one bounded piece of sound or animation. Playback presents that prepared piece over time. A silent GIF can show speech motion without carrying the actual voice.

These are voice labels mentioned in Verona's setup or tests, not people present in the session. Installed engine choices determine which voices are available. A voice label does not automatically choose a head's geometry or prove a human identity.
Runtime is the app while it is actually working. A process is one running program; its PID is a temporary number tag. An old PID in a receipt does not prove that program is still alive today.

A head is one running face instance; its session owns settings and jobs. The manager keeps the roster, and a host runs a face. Workers handle specific jobs, like a backstage crew with separate baskets.

Technical ownership says which component may change or close a resource. Isolation keeps test work from disturbing the user's app. Two different windows or ports alone do not prove their baskets, files and devices are separate.

RAM is the computer's temporary worktable. A working set measures memory currently resident for a process. A sleeping head can stop drawing while leaving its large model on the table, ready to speak again.

A cache keeps something already prepared so it is quicker next time. Lazy loading waits until it is needed. Latest-only keeps just the newest useful tray, not an ever-growing cupboard of every past face or utterance.

A resource is something the app uses, such as a buffer or process. Allocating reserves it; releasing gives it back. 'Release' can also mean publishing a software version: the sentence tells us which meaning is intended.

A boolean is yes or no. A default is the starting choice; opt-in means you deliberately choose yes. Immutable means fixed after creation. Think of choosing a puppet's special mode before opening its little theater.

The user interface, or UI, is what you click; user experience, or UX, is how using it feels. Metadata describes an item, such as its voice style. A visible checkbox must agree with the real setting backstage.

A command-line interface, or CLI, lets you type instructions. A flag is an extra named option. An agent is a program acting on instructions; it does not mean a human is inside the terminal moving the face.

Electron puts web-style drawing inside a desktop app. Edge is a browser. The document object model, or DOM, is the browser's organized page tree. Testing that tree is useful, but a picture can still need visual inspection.

An application programming interface, or API, is a menu of requests programs understand. HTTP carries many web requests; a route chooses which request handler answers. It is like ordering one item from a little local service counter.

Local means on this machine; offline means no internet is needed for that task. Loopback talks back to the same computer. Cloud services run elsewhere. A local page can still request remote content unless that behavior is deliberately prevented.

A capability is a secret ticket allowing particular API actions. Authentication checks permission. A sandbox limits what a program may do. Never put the secret ticket in a book, and do not confuse a local address with permission to act.

Inter-process communication, or IPC, passes notes between running programs. A callback runs when a promised event occurs. Polling repeatedly asks for news, like knocking on a door every moment instead of waiting for the bell.

An error means something did not work. A fallback is another path; stale data is out of date. A race happens when timing changes who wins. Verona should show failures, not quietly hand you an empty bowl labeled success.

A warm model is already loaded and waiting, like a kettle already prepared for tea. A cold start must load and set things up first. Keeping it warm can save waiting time while still using substantial memory.

A browser profile holds its own settings and saved state. Private data must not sneak into public artifacts. Credentials, including a personal access token or PAT, are secret keys; a test should use its own clean profile, not borrow yours.

An atomic switch replaces the visible result as one completed change, not half an old page and half a new one. Asynchronous work finishes later. A cancellation token is a little 'this job is no longer wanted' marker.

groups.title: Proof, tests and careful little promises

terms.explanation: A test asks a specific question. An assertion is its 'this must be true' rule. A regression test keeps an old bug from sneaking back. Passing a small checklist does not answer every question about the whole app.

A fixture is prepared test material; a harness sets up and observes the test. Think of a little practice stage. It must test the real behavior it claims, rather than a cardboard button that never calls the app.

Qualification says what a bounded technical check established on a particular setup. Acceptance is a person's judgment against the intended need. A passing test is a gold star for that test, not the owner's signature on every design.

A benchmark measures a specific workload. Counterbalancing changes the comparison order to reduce order effects. An outlier is an unusually different result. One good average is not a promise that every frame or machine will behave the same way.

A receipt records what a run did. Evidence supports a particular claim; provenance says where an artifact came from. A receipt is a dated footprint, not proof that the program is still running or that deleted raw frames still exist.

A baseline is the reference you compare against. A witness is a selected point or sample that should survive a change. A tolerance allows a justified small difference, not a bigger loophole added because a test was inconvenient.

A test matrix crosses choices such as head, view and mouth policy. Each combination is a case, like one square on a picnic checklist. Covering every square does not cover every possible sound, pose or computer.

An exact comparison asks whether selected bytes or pixels match. A timeline check compares decoded animation pictures at the intended times. These can catch changed output, but cannot by themselves decide whether a face looks kind, natural or correct.

Visual review means actually looking at the result. A contact sheet places several pictures together; a close-up magnifies a detail. Looking at selected stills is not the same as watching every frame or hearing the sound.

Scope says what a claim includes. A constraint is a rule it must obey; a tradeoff gives something up to gain something else. Inherited evidence comes from an earlier run; superseded means a newer decision replaces it.

A prototype tries an idea; an experiment asks a bounded question. Production is the supported app path. Integration connects pieces into it; parity means matching specified behavior. A promising review candidate has not automatically graduated into the supported app.

A capture records an actual output; a report arranges results for inspection. A reference guides comparison or appearance. A screenshot is one still moment, not evidence that an entire animation was watched or that a reference was matched exactly.

groups.title: Files, versions and the book itself

terms.explanation: Git keeps snapshots of source work. A repository is the project plus its history; a checkout is the files you are editing now. The project can also contain ignored local models and captures that are not in Git.

A commit labels a saved snapshot and its parents. A tree lists folders and files; a blob stores file content. A revision names one saved point. These are library catalog records, not evidence that the saved code ran successfully.

A branch follows a line of work; a tag labels a chosen saved version. A source cutoff says where this book's historical story stops. Adding an appendix does not move the old milestones or rewrite their dates.

A worktree is another checked-out workspace sharing Git history. Detached means it points to a commit rather than a branch. An ancestor is an earlier linked commit. Shared history does not make unique uncommitted edits safe to throw away.

GitHub hosts the repository. Issues record tasks; a Project board organizes them. Pushing sends commits to the remote host. Uploading code, publishing a PDF and deploying an app are different actions, not one big automatic button.

A manifest is an explicit packing list. An allowlist names what may enter; an inventory records what is there. A book's list helps keep private files out, like checking every item before closing a picnic basket.

A hash is a compact fingerprint of file bytes. SHA-256 is the fingerprint recipe; a checksum list records expected fingerprints. Matching fingerprints help confirm unchanged content, but do not prove the content is safe, accurate or approved.

A version names a state; a candidate is still being checked. A frozen edition is a preserved book snapshot. Portable inputs let the book be rebuilt elsewhere with its stated tools, without promising that every new PDF has identical bytes.

An artifact is an output; an asset is an ingredient. A file derivative is made from another item; in math, a derivative instead measures change. An archive bundles files. A tiny receipt is not every large working payload.

JSON is structured text; binary is a byte-based file representation. GLB packs a glTF 3D scene, while ONNX describes a neural computation. A Maya ASCII scene is text, but can contain commands: Verona parses required numbers and never executes it.

PNG stores a still picture, including transparency. GIF stores limited-color pictures and can animate, but has no audio track. ZIP bundles files together. A speaking GIF here is a silent visual preview, not a sound recording.

PDF keeps fixed book pages; HTML is the browser-readable companion. A bookmark jumps to a section. An anchor marks an exact spot, and a hotspot is a clickable area. This appendix gives technical words their own little landing pads.

A font draws letters called glyphs; Unicode identifies the characters. Embedding puts allowed letter shapes inside a PDF. PyMuPDF builds this book and Pillow handles its images. Pretty letters must still copy and search as the correct words.

Files are stored as bytes, little numbered pieces. CRLF uses two particular bytes to mark a line ending. A file can look the same after line endings change while its exact bytes and hash become different.

A license says how someone allows their work to be used. Attribution gives credit. Redistribution means sharing copies onward. Different code, model weights, fonts and recordings can have different rules; one friendly license does not cover the whole basket.

A dependency is a tool or library another job needs. Pinned means its version is fixed. An SDK is a development toolkit; a pipeline is a sequence of steps. Python and JavaScript are programming languages; Node runs JavaScript outside the browser.

terms.term: cm / ms / MB / MiB / GiB / percent
terms.explanation: cm measures centimeters; ms means thousandths of a second. MB is one million bytes; MiB is 1,048,576 bytes; GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes. Percent means out of one hundred. Always check which little measuring cup a number uses.

A junction or symlink points to another location, like a signpost rather than another box. Following it during deletion can reach shared data. Logical size adds file bytes; actual disk space can differ because of allocation or compression.

Source code is the written recipe for a program. An implementation is the actual working version of an idea. A function is a named little job; a script runs instructions. Merely writing the recipe does not prove the cake came out right.

A README is the project's welcome note. A journal explains what happened and why; a ledger keeps dated records. Chronology puts events in order. A timestamp dates a recorded event, not necessarily every image shown beside it.

Blender is a 3D authoring tool. Import reads an outside file into a chosen workflow. Static geometry is a shape without its own changing pose. It still needs a suitable movement method before becoming a convincing talking puppet.

ELI5 means 'explain like I'm five': start with familiar, friendly ideas instead of assuming expert knowledge. An analogy compares an unfamiliar thing with something familiar. Our puppets and picnic baskets explain mechanisms; they are not literal descriptions of the computer.

groups.title: Who's who in Verona's toy theater

terms.explanation: Claire and Mark name different underlying speech-motion identities with matching model assets. MPFB refers to a separate native-head toolchain and transfer route. Putting a different painted outfit on Claire does not turn her network into Mark's.

These are names used in Verona's head comparisons, not separate apps. Onyx maps to male-sharp. Their geometry and motion routes differ; a name alone does not specify a person's gender, voice or performance guarantee.

terms.term: Lyra / Elara / Mira / Selene / Neris / Thalia
terms.explanation: These are six separate review candidates from three supplied heads. Each pair compares preserving the supplied topology with reshaping Claire's topology. They are choices to inspect, not automatically installed production heads.

Akari is Verona's original Claire-based anime-style study, with coordinated face, eyes and hair. VRoid and VRM are outside avatar tools/formats researched as references. Their documentation is not permission to copy a character or proof Akari is production-ready.

A workstream is one bounded piece of work, labeled vr-NN. A milestone is a meaningful checkpoint; M1 is the first major one. IST here means India Standard Time, UTC+05:30, used to date commits consistently.
